case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ACCA’s definition of a prior state “serious drug offense” is measured against the federal controlled-substance schedules as they existed at the time of the prior state offense, the later federal firearm offense, or federal sentencing.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA), 18 U.S.C. § 924(e), specifically § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) (definition of “serious drug offense” referencing substances “controlled under” the Controlled Substances Act).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that ACCA’s cross-reference to substances “controlled under” federal law should be pegged to a single, administrable time—at least no later than the federal firearm offense date (and in petitioners’ broader framing, tied to the federal schedules in effect at the time of the federal offense, not the time of the prior state conviction). Under that approach, a state drug conviction does not qualify if it covered substances that were not federally controlled at the relevant federal-time benchmark, preventing defendants from receiving ACCA’s 15-year mandatory minimum based on outdated or now-removed substances and promoting uniformity, fair notice, and alignment with ACCA’s recidivism-focused purpose.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that ACCA’s “serious drug offense” inquiry should use the federal controlled-substance schedules in effect at the time the defendant committed the prior state drug crime (or otherwise at the time of that prior conviction), so that the federal enhancement turns on what the defendant actually did when it was done and avoids making ACCA predicates fluctuate based on later federal rescheduling decisions. The government also emphasizes administrability and consistency with ACCA’s backward-looking focus on prior convictions, contending that tying the inquiry to later federal-schedule changes would create arbitrary disparities depending on the happenstance of when a defendant is federally prosecuted or sentenced.
key_precedents: Martinez v. Attorney General, 906 F.3d 281 (3d Cir. 2018)
United States v. Marrero, 743 F.3d 389 (3d Cir. 2014)
United States v. Herrick, 545 F.3d 53 (1st Cir. 2008)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fair-notice and “current federal schedules” argument is the most serious point for Petitioner, but ACCA’s recidivist trigger—whether the defendant “has three previous convictions” for an offense “involving” a CSA-controlled substance—reads most naturally as a backward-looking classification of what those past convictions were at the time they were incurred. As Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, a federal-offense/sentencing-date benchmark would make ACCA exposure fluctuate with later rescheduling and the happenstance of federal charging timing, a particularly troubling instability for a mandatory-minimum regime. McNeill, though addressing a different clause, supports the interpretive principle that ACCA predicates are assessed by reference to the legal characteristics at the time of the prior conviction/offense, not later legal changes, and nothing in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii)’s cross-reference clearly displaces that default temporal anchor. Under a minimalist, legitimacy-preserving approach, the narrowest and most administrable holding is that the relevant CSA schedules are those in effect when the prior state drug offense/conviction occurred, leaving broader questions about retroactivity of federal descheduling to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that an incorporation of substances “controlled under” the CSA might ordinarily track the schedules as they exist when the federal consequence attaches, avoiding reliance on outdated classifications. But the enacted text asks whether the defendant “has three previous convictions” for an offense “involving” a controlled substance—language that is backward-looking and keyed to the historical conviction, and (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize) it supplies no clear forward-looking benchmark like the federal-offense or sentencing date. McNeill, though addressing a different clause, reinforces the recidivist-statute principle that predicate status is assessed as of the time the prior conviction was incurred, preventing ACCA exposure from fluctuating with later executive rescheduling or prosecutorial timing, a concern Justice Gorsuch rightly frames as rule-of-law and separation-of-powers adjacent. Under an original public meaning/textualist approach, absent a clear statement that Congress meant a moving federal schedule to retroactively recharacterize past convictions, I cannot adopt Petitioner’s dynamic rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fair-notice and “current federal law” intuition is the most serious counterargument, but it treats the CSA cross-reference as a dynamic switch that retroactively reclassifies old convictions—something ACCA’s backward-looking structure (“has three previous convictions”) does not naturally support. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a federal-offense or sentencing-date rule would make ACCA eligibility fluctuate with later Executive rescheduling decisions and prosecutorial timing, producing arbitrary disparities incompatible with a mandatory-minimum recidivist scheme. McNeill, though addressing the maximum-penalty clause, reinforces the broader temporal principle that we evaluate predicate convictions by the legal regime at the time they were incurred, avoiding the instability Sotomayor’s approach would introduce. Under a textualist reading, nothing in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) clearly commands a moving federal benchmark, and absent that clear statement we should not let later policy shifts erase historically serious drug-trafficking convictions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize ACCA’s backward-looking focus on whether a defendant “has” prior convictions, and their administrability concerns are real. But that structural point does not answer the separate textual question embedded in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii): whether the prior offense involved a substance “controlled under” the CSA—a cross-reference that, in ordinary legal usage, most naturally tracks the federal schedules as they exist when the federal enhancement attaches, absent a clear statement freezing an incorporated federal list. McNeill, as Justice Thomas invokes it, underscores that ACCA often looks to historical facts about past convictions, but it dealt with a static state maximum-penalty inquiry and does not compel reading a dynamically maintained federal definitional list as time-locked. Under a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, I cannot accept a rule that imposes today’s 15-year mandatory minimum based on substances the federal government has since determined should not be controlled, particularly where the contrary rule better aligns notice and proportionality with the moment federal punishment is imposed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (and Justice Jackson) make the best point for Petitioner: an incorporation of substances “controlled under” the CSA can read naturally as a dynamic reference to current federal schedules, and that has a fair-notice/proportionality appeal in a mandatory-minimum context. But ACCA’s operative inquiry—whether the defendant “has” three “previous convictions” for an offense “involving” such a substance—works most coherently when the federal definition is used to classify the historical conviction as of the time it was incurred, otherwise predicate status turns on later charging/sentencing timing and post hoc rescheduling. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern is not just policy; it is a structural reading of a recidivist statute that is meant to be stable rather than a moving target. And while McNeill is not mechanically on all fours, it reinforces the same backward-looking temporal logic for ACCA predicates, absent a clear textual instruction that Congress meant this CSA cross-reference to fluctuate over time.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point for Petitioner: that the CSA cross-reference to substances “controlled under” federal law sounds like a dynamic incorporation applied when the federal consequence attaches, with fair-notice and proportionality intuitions. But ACCA’s operative inquiry—whether the defendant “has three previous convictions” for an offense “involving” a federally defined controlled substance—is structurally backward-looking, and as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, McNeill’s temporal logic for recidivist statutes confirms we ordinarily assess predicate status by the legal regime at the time of the prior conviction to avoid eligibility “fluctuat[ing]” with later changes. Petitioners’ moving-benchmark rule would let subsequent Executive scheduling decisions and prosecutorial timing alter a mandatory-minimum consequence tied to past convictions, a separation-of-powers and rule-of-law problem absent a clear textual command. Because § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) provides no explicit forward-looking temporal marker, the best textualist reading anchors the CSA definition to the time the prior conviction was incurred.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fair-notice and “current federal schedules” point is the best argument for Petitioner, but in a recidivist statute the key inquiry is backward-looking—whether the defendant “has three previous convictions”—so it is a poor fit to let later federal rescheduling retroactively alter the character of those historical convictions. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Petitioner’s approach would make ACCA exposure turn on prosecutorial timing and later Executive/Congress action, producing instability and arbitrariness that Congress is unlikely to have intended for a mandatory-minimum scheme. McNeill, although addressing a different clause, reinforces the interpretive principle (as Justice Kagan emphasizes) that ACCA predicate status is assessed as of the prior conviction/offense to avoid fluctuations from subsequent legal changes. Under an institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, the most administrable and coherent reading is that the CSA cross-reference is applied as of the time of the prior drug offense/conviction, not the time of the federal firearm case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the CSA cross-reference could be read as a dynamic incorporation, keyed to the schedules in effect when the federal consequence attaches, and that this better matches ordinary intuitions about “current law” and notice. But ACCA’s operative language—whether the defendant “has three previous convictions” for an offense “involving” a substance “controlled under” the CSA—reads as a backward-looking classification of historical convictions, and as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a moving federal-schedule benchmark would make predicate status fluctuate with later rescheduling and charging timing in a way that sits uneasily with a recidivist enhancement. McNeill, though not mechanically controlling, reinforces that interpretive premise: ACCA “concerns itself with convictions that have already occurred,” and absent a clear textual signal, I would not adopt a rule that retroactively recharacterizes those convictions based on subsequent federal policy shifts. Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concerns are real, but under a textualist methodology they cannot supply the missing temporal anchor, and the instability her rule introduces is a significant structural objection.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability concern that ACCA should not “fluctuate” with later scheduling or charging timing, but that stability interest cannot override the separate statutory requirement that the prior offense involve a substance “controlled under” federal law—a cross-reference that, in ordinary legal usage, tracks current federal definitions when the federal consequence attaches. McNeill, as the Chief and Justice Kavanaugh invoke it, is relevant as a recidivist-temporality precedent, but it dealt with a fixed historical attribute (state maximum penalty at the time) rather than a dynamically maintained federal list Congress designed to be updated; that difference matters when we ask what Congress meant by incorporating the CSA schedules. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers worry cuts both ways: freezing an obsolete federal schedule allows past executive classifications—since repudiated—to impose today’s 15-year mandatory minimum, a practical fairness and proportionality problem that my methodology weighs heavily absent clear congressional direction to do so. Given ACCA’s severity and the lack of a clear statutory command to lock in outdated federal schedules, I remain with Petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: ACCA asks whether the defendant “has three previous convictions” for a “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), a backward-looking inquiry that is most naturally evaluated as of the time of the prior state offense/conviction rather than fluctuating with later federal rescheduling. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), though addressing maximum-penalty timing, reinforces that ACCA predicates turn on the legal status of the prior conviction at the time it was incurred, not on subsequent legal changes, which promotes administrability and avoids arbitrary disparities based on when federal prosecution or sentencing occurs. Reading § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii)’s reference to substances “controlled under” the CSA to incorporate later schedule changes would make predicate status depend on post hoc federal amendments rather than the defendant’s past criminal conduct, undermining ACCA’s recidivist design and risking instability in sentencing. A narrow, precedent-consistent rule pegged to the time of the prior offense/conviction best preserves uniform application within ACCA’s framework and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of ACCA asks whether the defendant "has three previous convictions" for a "serious drug offense," 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), and defines that term by reference to an offense "involving manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to manufacture or distribute, a controlled substance (as defined in section 102 of the Controlled Substances Act)," § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii). That backward-looking focus on the prior conviction is best read to incorporate the federal schedules as they existed when the defendant committed the prior state drug crime, not as later amended, because the predicate turns on what the defendant previously did and was convicted of. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), likewise treated ACCA predicates as measured at the time of the prior state offense/conviction rather than by later changes in law, and nothing in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii)’s cross-reference clearly commands a moving, prosecution-date or sentencing-date benchmark. Tying qualification to later federal rescheduling would make ACCA’s mandatory minimum hinge on subsequent federal policy shifts rather than the original public meaning of "previous convictions" in a recidivist statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: ACCA asks whether the defendant "has three previous convictions" for a "serious drug offense," 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), and that backward-looking structure points to evaluating the predicate based on the law as it existed when the prior drug crime was committed/convicted rather than allowing later federal rescheduling to erase a conviction’s status. The phrase in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) requiring that the offense involve a substance "controlled under" the CSA is best read as a cross-reference to the federal definition at the time of the prior conduct, because ACCA’s recidivist focus is on what the defendant previously did and was convicted of, not on subsequent policy changes. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), supports this temporal approach by emphasizing that ACCA predicate inquiries look to the historical facts and legal regime governing the prior conviction to avoid making enhancements turn on later legislative changes and prosecutorial happenstance. Pegging the CSA schedules to federal offense or sentencing would create arbitrary disparities depending on when federal charges are brought and would undermine ACCA’s incapacitative purpose by allowing later rescheduling to negate otherwise qualifying prior drug-trafficking convictions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: ACCA’s text defines a “serious drug offense” by reference to substances “controlled under” the Controlled Substances Act, 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), and that cross-reference most naturally points to the federal schedules as they exist at the time the federal firearm offense (or, at latest, federal sentencing) occurs—when the federal consequence attaches and fair notice matters. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), is not to the contrary: it addressed a different clause (the “maximum term of imprisonment … prescribed by law”) and required looking back to the state maximum at the time of the prior conviction, not freezing an external, dynamically updated federal definitional list like the CSA schedules. Treating long-superseded federal schedules as controlling would make a 15-year mandatory minimum turn on obsolete classifications and would fall hardest on vulnerable defendants in the criminal system, contrary to ACCA’s recidivism rationale and basic fairness. Using the federal-time benchmark also promotes administrability and national uniformity by tying the enhancement to the federal law in force when the federal prosecution is triggered, rather than to shifting historical federal schedules embedded in decades-old state convictions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) asks whether the defendant “has” prior “serious drug offense” convictions, a backward-looking recidivist inquiry that naturally measures the state offense against the federal benchmark as it existed when the prior crime was committed (or at least when the conviction occurred), rather than letting later federal rescheduling retroactively change the character of that past conviction. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), though addressing changes in state law, reinforces that ACCA predicates are assessed by looking to the law as it stood at the time of the prior offense/conviction to avoid “absurd results” and sentencing disparities driven by later legal developments. Tying the CSA cross-reference to the time of federal firearm offense or sentencing would make ACCA eligibility turn on happenstance timing of federal prosecution and subsequent administrative scheduling decisions—an unworkable regime that undermines statutory coherence and ACCA’s incapacitation purpose. Reading “controlled under” in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) to incorporate the schedules contemporaneous with the prior state drug offense yields a stable, administrable rule consistent with ACCA’s structure and the Court’s approach to temporal measurement in recidivist enhancements.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) asks whether the prior state offense “involv[ed] … a controlled substance (as defined in section 102 of the Controlled Substances Act),” a backward-looking inquiry focused on what the defendant was convicted of doing, not on later federal scheduling changes. As in McNeill v. United States, ACCA predicate determinations ordinarily look to the law and facts as they existed at the time of the prior conviction; tying the enhancement to later rescheduling would make predicate status “fluctuate” based on post hoc federal actions and prosecutorial timing, an odd fit for a recidivist statute. Reading the cross-reference to incorporate later amendments would also raise serious fair-notice and separation-of-powers concerns by effectively letting the Executive’s scheduling decisions retroactively expand or contract mandatory minimum exposure for past conduct. At minimum, where the statute does not clearly specify a later benchmark, the more administrable, historically anchored reading consistent with McNeill should govern.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: ACCA’s definition of a “serious drug offense” is a backward-looking inquiry focused on the defendant’s prior convictions, and the most workable, historically grounded reading is to measure the CSA schedules as they existed when the defendant committed the prior state drug crime (or at least when the prior conviction became final). McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), though addressing maximum penalties, reflects the same core principle that ACCA predicates are assessed based on the law in effect at the time of the prior offense/conviction, not later legal changes, and that approach avoids making ACCA eligibility fluctuate with subsequent federal rescheduling. Tying the CSA cross-reference in 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) to later federal-schedule changes would introduce arbitrariness based on prosecution/sentencing timing and undermine administrability and consistent national application. Consistent with judicial restraint and preserving ACCA’s practical workability, I would adhere to a time-of-prior-offense (or time-of-prior-conviction) benchmark for the federal schedules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) asks whether the defendant has a prior conviction for an offense “involving” a substance “controlled under” the CSA, a backward-looking inquiry that naturally takes the law as it existed when the predicate offense was committed and adjudicated, not as later rescheduled. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), though addressing “maximum term of imprisonment,” reinforces that ACCA predicates are assessed by reference to the state offense’s legal characteristics at the time of the prior conviction, because ACCA “concerns itself with convictions that have already occurred.” Pegging the CSA schedules to federal offense or sentencing would make predicate status turn on happenstance timing and later regulatory change rather than the defendant’s prior criminal conduct, in tension with ACCA’s recidivism-focused structure. Precedent and methodological consistency thus favor using the federal schedules as they existed at the time of the prior state drug offense/conviction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: ACCA’s definition of “serious drug offense” in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) turns on whether the state offense involved a substance “controlled under” federal law, and that cross-reference most sensibly uses the federal schedules in effect at least by the time of the federal firearm offense, when the defendant’s enhanced federal exposure attaches and fair notice concerns are at their height. Pegging the inquiry to that federal-time benchmark promotes administrable uniformity and avoids imposing ACCA’s 15-year mandatory minimum based on substances Congress (or the Executive under delegated authority) has since removed from federal control, which has substantial practical consequences for sentencing severity. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), is distinguishable because it addressed how to determine a prior offense’s “maximum term of imprisonment” under then-existing state law, not the temporal meaning of an incorporated federal drug schedule; it therefore does not compel using an obsolete federal schedule for the “controlled under” inquiry. Given ACCA’s severe penalty and the Court’s insistence on clear, workable rules in this area (see Johnson v. United States, 576 U.S. 591 (2015)), the statute should not be read to make the enhancement hinge on historical federal schedules disconnected from the federal prosecution triggering the mandatory minimum.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a “serious drug offense” under ACCA by comparing the state drug definition to the federal controlled-substance schedules as they existed at the time of the prior state offense, the later federal firearm offense, or federal sentencing.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA), 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) (definition of “serious drug offense”), incorporating by reference the federal controlled-substance schedules under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that ACCA’s “serious drug offense” inquiry should use the federal controlled-substance schedules in effect at the time of the federal firearm offense (or, alternatively, at federal sentencing), so that ACCA’s mandatory 15-year enhancement does not hinge on outdated federal drug scheduling decisions; using current (or at least federal-offense-time) schedules better aligns with ACCA’s recidivism rationale, avoids irrational disparities, and prevents enhancing sentences based on substances that federal law no longer treats as controlled.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that the ACCA predicate determination should be anchored to the federal controlled-substance schedules in effect at the time of the defendant’s prior state drug crime/conviction, because ACCA asks whether the defendant “has” prior qualifying convictions and the categorical comparison should reflect the law defining those earlier offenses; this approach is said to be consistent with ACCA’s backward-looking structure and Supreme Court precedent emphasizing that ACCA looks to the historical fact of the prior conviction, not subsequent legal changes.
key_precedents: Martinez v. Attorney General, 906 F.3d 281 (3d Cir. 2018)
United States v. Marrero, 743 F.3d 389 (3d Cir. 2014)
United States v. Herrick, 545 F.3d 53 (1st Cir. 2008)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/lenity argument presses the hardest point: that we are imposing a present federal penalty and ordinarily apply current federal definitions, so it seems anomalous to enhance based on substances later removed from the CSA. But ACCA’s text and structure frame the inquiry as whether the defendant “has” three “previous convictions,” and as Justice Thomas (invoking McNeill) emphasizes, the predicate inquiry is inherently historical—later legal developments do not silently rewrite what a prior conviction was for ACCA purposes. Justice Jackson’s effort to cabin McNeill to the state-maximum-penalty clause does not overcome the broader principle McNeill articulates: the “only way to answer” a backward-looking predicate question is to consult the law at the time of the prior conviction, rather than making ACCA’s reach depend on subsequent federal scheduling changes. On a minimalist approach, we can decide only the timing of the CSA-schedule comparator under § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), leaving other ACCA predicate issues for another day and preserving administrable, precedent-consistent lines.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson most forcefully argue that the CSA cross-reference is a present-tense federal definition applied when we impose today’s penalty, and that temporal silence plus ACCA’s severity triggers lenity. But the text asks whether the defendant “has” three “previous convictions,” and § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) identifies those convictions by what the prior offense “involv[ed]”—a necessarily historical inquiry into the completed conviction, consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s reading and with McNeill’s rejection of predicates “disappearing” due to later legal change. Treating later CSA rescheduling as controlling would make ACCA’s application depend on post hoc executive scheduling decisions rather than the fact and nature of the prior conviction, a mismatch with a recidivist enhancement absent clear congressional instruction. Because that structure yields a determinate backward-looking rule, I do not see the kind of grievous ambiguity that would justify lenity here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s argument that the CSA cross-reference is a present-tense federal definition applied when we impose today’s penalty is the strongest point for Petitioner, but it still lacks a textual signal in § 924(e)(1)–(2) overcoming the statute’s backward-looking focus on whether the defendant “has” “previous convictions.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, McNeill’s core interpretive logic is that ACCA predicates are determined as historical facts; letting later CSA rescheduling alter predicate status would make the enhancement turn on post hoc executive action and timing happenstance, not the defendant’s recidivist record. Justice Jackson’s delegation point does not answer the temporal question: Congress’s choice to incorporate the CSA does not imply that later administrative revisions silently rewrite the effect of final convictions absent clear direction, especially given ACCA’s express carveouts elsewhere (e.g., § 921(a)(20)). Because the text and structure point to a stable time-of-prior-conviction benchmark, I do not see the grievous ambiguity needed to invoke lenity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize ACCA’s backward-looking phrasing (“has three previous convictions”) and the administrability appeal of a fixed temporal anchor, but that point goes to identifying the historical conviction, not to freezing the separate federal definitional cross-reference that determines whether we impose today’s extraordinary 15-year minimum. McNeill, as Justice Thomas reads it, squarely answers that we consult the law at the time of the prior conviction for state-law maximum penalties; it does not compel importing an atextual “time-of-prior-conviction” rule for the CSA schedules, where Congress used a federal definitional incorporation that sentencing courts ordinarily apply as federal law currently stands absent clear instruction. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern about later executive scheduling is mitigated by Congress’s own choice to define the predicate by reference to the CSA—delegated scheduling is the mechanism Congress selected, and the harder fairness problem is locking defendants into ACCA based on substances the federal government no longer controls. Given the statute’s temporal silence on the CSA comparator and ACCA’s severity, I still see sufficient ambiguity to apply lenity and choose the rule that avoids imposing a mandatory minimum based on obsolete federal drug policy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest counterpoint: that the CSA cross-reference looks like a present-tense federal definition applied at the time we impose today’s penalty, and that temporal silence plus ACCA’s severity should trigger lenity. But the surrounding text in § 924(e)(1)–(2) is recidivist and backward-looking (“has three previous convictions”), and—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize—McNeill’s core interpretive move is that predicate status is a historical question that later legal changes do not silently rewrite absent clear instruction. Freezing the CSA comparator at the time of the prior conviction best preserves statutory coherence and avoids making ACCA’s reach depend on later (often executive) rescheduling decisions that create happenstance disparities among similarly situated defendants. Because the text and structure point to a stable historical anchor, I do not see the kind of grievous ambiguity that would justify lenity here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that the CSA cross-reference looks like a present federal definitional inquiry applied when we impose today’s federal penalty, and that McNeill addressed only changes in state law, not federal scheduling. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, ACCA’s text is structured around a backward-looking recidivist question—whether the defendant “has” three “previous convictions” for an offense “involving” a federally controlled substance—and McNeill’s core interpretive point is that the only sensible way to answer such a question is to evaluate the predicate as it existed when incurred, rather than letting later legal changes make it “disappear.” Justice Jackson’s response that Congress chose CSA delegation does not solve the temporal problem; reading ACCA to incorporate later executive rescheduling would still make the reach of a mandatory minimum turn on post hoc administrative action without a clear textual command. Given that structure and precedent, the statute is not grievously ambiguous, so lenity cannot do the work Petitioners ask of it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: absent an express temporal hook, the CSA cross-reference can look like a present-tense federal definition applied at the time of the federal firearm offense, and fairness/lenity concerns are acute given ACCA’s 15-year minimum. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, ACCA’s operative inquiry is backward-looking—whether the defendant “has” three “previous convictions”—and McNeill’s core interpretive logic applies beyond state maximum-penalty changes: predicate status is determined by the legal regime at the time of the prior conviction unless Congress clearly provides otherwise. Treating later CSA scheduling changes as silently altering the federal consequences of final convictions would create a moving target driven by subsequent regulatory updates and undermine administrability and uniformity, while Congress elsewhere provided explicit mechanisms (e.g., § 921(a)(20)) for when later events negate predicate effect. Under an institutionalist, precedent- and text-centered approach, I do not see genuine ambiguity sufficient to trigger lenity here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best counter: that the CSA cross-reference looks like a present-tense federal definition applied when we impose today’s penalty, and that ACCA’s severity plus temporal silence triggers lenity. But § 924(e)(1)–(2) is structured as a recidivist enhancement keyed to whether the defendant “has” “previous convictions,” and as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, McNeill’s core interpretive logic is that predicate status is assessed under the legal regime governing the prior conviction unless Congress clearly provides otherwise. Nothing in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii)’s incorporation of the CSA schedules supplies a timing rule that would let later federal scheduling changes retroactively strip a conviction of predicate effect, and ACCA’s express treatment of when convictions are disregarded elsewhere (e.g., § 921(a)(20)) cuts against inferring a silent, schedule-based retroactivity. Because the text and structure yield a determinate backward-looking rule, I do not think lenity can do the work Petitioners ask of it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability point—ACCA is recidivist and backward-looking, so predicates should be assessed under the law at the time of conviction—squarely presents the hardest counterargument. But as Justice Sotomayor notes, § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) does not ask a purely historical question about the state offense alone; it adds a present federal definitional filter (“controlled substance (as defined in” the CSA)) that functions like an incorporated federal definition the sentencing court applies when imposing today’s federal consequence. McNeill, invoked by Justice Thomas and Justice Alito, is materially different because the statutory phrase there (“maximum term … prescribed by law”) is itself temporally anchored to the prior conviction’s penalty regime, whereas the CSA cross-reference is not, and reading it as frozen risks imposing a mandatory 15-year minimum for conduct that federal law no longer treats as involving a controlled substance. Given that temporal silence, the severe practical consequences, and the need for procedurally fair notice when federal law has changed, I continue to think lenity and fairness favor using the CSA schedules operative at the time of the federal firearm offense (or at latest sentencing), notwithstanding the moving-target concerns emphasized by Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch.

John Roberts.reasoning: ACCA’s definition of “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), operates in a backward-looking way by asking whether a defendant “has” prior qualifying convictions, and our ACCA cases generally treat the predicate inquiry as turning on the historical fact of the prior conviction rather than subsequent legal developments. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), while addressing changes in state law, reflects the same basic approach: courts assess the predicate based on the law governing that prior offense at the relevant time, to avoid making ACCA’s application depend on later legislative or administrative revisions. Anchoring the CSA-schedule comparison to the time of the prior state conviction also promotes administrability and uniformity in applying the categorical approach, limiting satellite litigation about later federal scheduling changes. Given the statute’s recidivist structure and the need for stable, narrow rules that preserve institutional legitimacy, I would affirm the time-of-prior-conviction framework absent a clearer congressional directive to the contrary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of ACCA asks whether the defendant “has” three prior convictions for a “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), and defines that term by reference to an “offense under State law” involving certain drug activity “for which a maximum term of imprisonment of ten years or more is prescribed by law,” § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), a backward-looking inquiry keyed to the historical fact of the prior conviction and the law that defined it. Consistent with McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816, 820–22 (2011), courts should not allow later legal changes to make a prior qualifying conviction “disappear” for ACCA purposes; the same logic applies when the incorporated federal schedules change after the state conviction. Petitioner's time-of-federal-offense or time-of-sentencing rule lacks a textual anchor in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) and would make the enhancement depend on happenstance timing of later federal regulatory updates rather than the defendant’s prior criminal conduct and conviction. Because ACCA is a recidivist statute focused on prior convictions, the relevant comparison to the CSA schedules is the version in effect at the time of the prior state offense/conviction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: ACCA’s text is backward-looking: it imposes the enhancement based on whether the defendant “has” prior convictions for a “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), which requires asking what the prior state offense involved when it was committed/convicted, not what federal schedules later became. As McNeill v. United States holds, the “only way to answer th[e] backward-looking question” about a “previous convictio[n]” is to consult the law applicable at the time of that conviction, and that logic applies equally to whether the substance at issue matched the CSA definition incorporated by § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii). The statute’s structure—treating predicates as historical facts and providing a specific rule for when convictions are disregarded (e.g., expungement under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(20))—cuts against treating later scheduling changes as silently erasing predicate status. Petitioner's approach would inject instability and sentencing disparities keyed to post hoc federal administrative updates, undermining ACCA’s practical operation and Congress’s evident recidivist design.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: ACCA defines a “serious drug offense” by incorporating the CSA schedules, 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), and the ordinary rule in criminal law is that liability and penalties turn on federal law as it exists when the federal firearm offense is committed, not on superseded federal classifications. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), does not compel the Government’s result because it addressed looking to historical state law to identify the elements and maximum punishment of the prior state conviction (step one), not which version of the federal CSA schedules supplies the federal comparator (step two). Anchoring the CSA schedules to the time of the federal firearm offense better fits ACCA’s recidivist rationale and avoids arbitrary, harsh disparities—imposing a mandatory 15-year minimum based on substances Congress and the Executive have since determined should not be federally controlled. Where the statute is at least ambiguous on timing, the rule of lenity and concerns about fairness to defendants facing drastic mandatory enhancements counsel using the federal schedules in effect at the time of the federal offense.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: ACCA’s text is backward-looking: it enhances sentences for defendants who “has three previous convictions” for a “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), and the most administrable reading is that the categorical comparison fixes both sides of the inquiry as of the time the prior conviction was incurred. McNeill v. United States supports that approach by insisting that ACCA predicates be evaluated based on the law that defined the prior offense at the time of conviction, rather than later legal changes, because the statute asks about the historical fact of a qualifying conviction. When ACCA incorporates the CSA schedules by reference in defining a “serious drug offense,” § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), that incorporation is best read to operate in the same temporally anchored way to avoid turning ACCA eligibility on later federal scheduling decisions unrelated to the defendant’s past conduct. This rule also promotes workability and coherence by preventing defendants with identical prior convictions from receiving different ACCA treatment depending on the happenstance of subsequent rescheduling between the prior conviction and federal sentencing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: ACCA asks whether the defendant “has three previous convictions” for a “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1), and defines that term by reference to offenses “involving” federally controlled substances, § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii); that backward-looking structure points to assessing the predicate conviction as it existed when it was incurred. McNeill v. United States instructs that ACCA predicates are evaluated by looking to the law at the time of the prior conviction to identify the offense’s elements and punishment, and the same historical approach best fits the incorporated federal schedules when determining whether the prior conviction corresponded to a federally controlled substance at that time. Using later schedules would make ACCA’s applicability turn on post hoc federal regulatory changes, inviting sentencing instability and raising separation-of-powers concerns by allowing executive rescheduling decisions to alter the consequences of already-final convictions. If there is any lingering ambiguity about the temporal reference, it is not enough to override ACCA’s text and structure, and McNeill supplies the governing interpretive framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: ACCA’s definition of “serious drug offense,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), is backward-looking and asks whether the defendant “has” prior qualifying convictions, so the categorical inquiry should be anchored to the law defining those prior offenses, including the federal CSA schedules as incorporated at that time. McNeill v. United States held that ACCA predicates are assessed by looking to the prior offense as it existed when committed/convicted, rejecting the notion that later legal changes retroactively alter whether a conviction counts, 563 U.S. at 820–23. That time-of-prior-offense approach is more workable and administrable and better fits ACCA’s recidivist design than a shifting, forward-looking standard tied to later federal scheduling changes. Absent clear congressional direction to make subsequent federal scheduling decisions retroactively control ACCA predicates, judicial restraint counsels adhering to McNeill’s framework and the statute’s historical focus.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) defines a “serious drug offense” by asking whether the defendant “has” a qualifying “previous conviction,” a backward-looking inquiry that naturally fixes the comparison at the time the prior state offense/conviction was incurred. Reading the statute textually, the federal schedules are incorporated as the definitional benchmark for what that prior conviction involved, and nothing in § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) directs courts to update that benchmark based on later changes to federal scheduling. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816, 820 (2011), though addressing ACCA’s penalty prong, rests on the same “previous conviction” focus and supports consulting the law that applied when the prior conviction occurred rather than subsequent legal changes. Anchoring the analysis to the prior-offense time also best fits ACCA’s recidivist structure and avoids making predicate status turn on post hoc federal administrative or legislative rescheduling unrelated to the historical fact of the prior conviction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: ACCA’s enhancement turns on whether the defendant “has” a prior conviction for an offense “involving … a controlled substance (as defined in” the CSA), 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(A)(ii), and that incorporation is best read to require a categorical comparison to the federal schedules as they exist at the time of the federal firearm offense (or, at latest, sentencing), when the federal court is deciding the present legal consequences of the prior conviction. McNeill v. United States, 563 U.S. 816 (2011), addressed a different textual hook—ACCA’s historical “maximum term of imprisonment” for the prior state offense—and does not compel importing a time-of-prior-offense rule into the CSA-schedules inquiry, which asks a “here-and-now” federal definitional question. Using current (or federal-offense-time) schedules better fits ACCA’s recidivism rationale and avoids imposing a mandatory 15-year minimum based on substances that federal law no longer treats as controlled, producing arbitrary disparities in similarly situated defendants. This reading also advances procedural fairness by making the enhancement’s trigger depend on the federal law operative when the defendant commits the federal firearm offense and is sentenced, rather than on subsequently superseded federal scheduling decisions.
